title: Cricket and the Shimmering Dewdrops
markdown:
Near the hidden terraces of Ferncrown, pine trees whispered to the wind and rocky paths wound like sleepy serpents. The air smelled of needles, damp earth, and a hint of wild berries. Cricket the young goblin lived there among his mountain woods companions, heart as warm as a hearth fire, eyes as bright as polished pebbles.

His days went with Flim, a squirrel whose tail was as expressive as a wagging dog’s, always twitching with curiosity; Moss, a toad whose quiet wisdom rumbled like distant thunder; and Pip, a bat of soft fur and velvety wings, perched on Cricket’s shoulder or tucked in the hood of a patched tunic. Flim chattered about the best nuts. Moss offered steady advice. Pip spoke in tiny earnest squeaks and nudges.

One fine morning the sun dappled the forest floor, painting shifting patterns of gold and emerald through the leaves. A perfect day for exploring. They ventured along a path they had not taken before, deeper into the whispering pines. The air was thick with damp soil, the sweet perfume of wild thyme, and the clean sharp aroma of pine. Pip stirred on Cricket’s shoulder and squeaked, as if to say: something new ahead. Something exciting.

Around ancient moss-covered boulders came a peculiar grumbling, like a badger who had lost a favourite berry. “Patience,” Moss whispered. “Let us see what troubles the air.”

In a small sunlit clearing sat Agnes the witch and Bartholomew the wizard, quite cross. Between them grew mushrooms unlike any they had seen, caps covered in tiny iridescent dewdrops that shimmered rainbow though the sun was high and there was no rain. Agnes pointed a gnarled finger. Bartholomew stroked a snowy beard.

“They are my shimmering dewdrops. I need them for moonbeam soup. It won’t be quite right without their gentle glow.”

“They are my glimmering orbs. Enchanted ink needs their sparkle to write the stars onto my maps. Without them the constellations will be dim.”

Cricket felt a pang for both: Agnes’s drooping shoulders, Bartholomew’s worried eyes. He did not see why they could not share, only that they were unhappy. Flim noticed how Agnes guarded her side, how Bartholomew reached and pulled back. Pip chirped, worried.

“We can help them. Let’s gather them. Then they can each have a pile.”

With the best of intentions they scurried. Flim plucked dewdrops with tiny paws. Moss scooped them into a large fallen leaf. Cricket tried to gather every mushroom, thinking a big pile would split easily, and nudged Pip to roll stray drops toward the leaf-basket.

Agnes and Bartholomew grew more flustered.

“That one was the perfect size for the moonbeam essence.”

“That one had the perfect shimmer for the constellation chart.”

The more they helped, the noisier the worry. Cricket stopped. The leaf overflowed, each drop winking. Agnes more creased than he had ever seen her. Bartholomew’s shoulders lower. Pip nudged his cheek.

“Ma,” Cricket whispered, a goblin way of asking for a careful moment. He had made things worse. Eager to help, he had not stopped to listen.

“Agnes. You need them for soup. Warmth and a gentle glow.” She nodded, eyes rainy. “Bartholomew. You need them for ink. To map the stars.” A sad nod, beard less grand. “If you both take all of them, there are none left. And the forest is full of shimmering things.”

Flim scampered up a tree and returned with a perfectly formed acorn cap filled with the clearest water from a hidden spring. “This water catches the light too. Maybe it can hold the sparkle for Bartholomew’s ink.”

Bartholomew held it to the sun. Tiny stars seemed to have fallen in. “It does hold the light. A touch of magic, and I won’t need quite so many mushrooms.”

Agnes’s watery smile. “If he needs fewer, there will be enough for soup. But my soup needs a special gentle shimmer. And your friends gathered them all.”

Cricket looked at the basket, the mushrooms, the vast green. “What if we don’t pick all of them? Only the ones Agnes needs now. When Bartholomew needs ink, he can ask us to gather more. And maybe we can find shimmering dewdrops on other plants for you both.”

Moss rumbled. Roots of an oak helping a whole forest: when they share, everyone benefits. He did not make a speech of it. He simply set the leaf down where both could reach.

Agnes chuckled, rustling leaves. “Perhaps we were getting a bit too worried about keeping them.”

“These little ones have shown us a better way.”

They helped Agnes gather just enough, leaving plenty for Bartholomew later. He waved a pouch of sparkling dust from the acorn-cap water into Agnes’s hands for extra flavour. She saved a few drops from a different mushroom for his ink: the perfect sparkle.

The grumbling ceased, replaced by the murmur of understanding and the chirping of birds. Cricket, Flim, Moss, and Pip waved goodbye to Agnes and Bartholomew, who were already chatting about enchanted quills and the secrets of fragrant soups. They walked toward home as the sun dipped below the peaks, painting orange, pink, and purple. Pip nested warm against Cricket’s neck. The dewdrops in the Ferncrown woods kept their shimmer, which was enough of a map, and enough of a soup, for one evening.
characters: Cricket (kind young goblin), Pip (a velvet bat)
